analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress, the president, and the vice president from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: A bill barring members of Congress, the president, and the vice president from owning or trading individual stocks drew 23 Senate backers and won committee approval, but the full Senate never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar members of Congress, the president, the vice president, and their spouses and young children from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and other non-diversified investments, and would require them to divest what they own within 120 days of starting a new term. Officials who failed to comply would face a fine equal to a month's pay or 10% of the un-divested holdings, repeating every 30 days. It would also set a $500 fine for each late trade disclosure and create a searchable public database of congressional financial filings. A Senate committee approved the bill in December 2024, but the full Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain a check on lawmakers' ability to buy and sell stocks in companies their own decisions affect, plus clearer public records of officials' finances. Rank-and-file members who already avoid trading conflicts gain a level playing field, since colleagues could no longer keep individual stock portfolios.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from purchasing or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and comparable derivatives — only diversified funds, Treasury securities, and a short list of other holdings are allowed.

Requires officials to divest those holdings within 120 days of starting a new term; the version reported by the committee also covers the president and vice president, adds cryptocurrency and other digital assets to the ban, and phases out the qualified blind trust escape hatch by requiring existing trusts to sell their stocks and dissolve.

Backs the ban with real teeth: a civil penalty equal to the greater of a month's pay or 10% of each un-divested investment, charged every 30 days noncompliance continues, plus a $500 fine for each late trade report under the existing STOCK Act.

Requires ethics offices to publish compliance certifications, trust documents, and penalty records online, and replaces paper financial disclosures with a searchable, downloadable public database that can be sorted by filer, asset, and transaction date.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the president, the vice president, and their families, who would have to sell off individual stock portfolios and could no longer hold crypto or derivatives; the bill extends an existing IRS deferral (section 1043) to cushion the tax hit when they sell. Congressional ethics offices would bear the cost of administering, publishing, and enforcing the new system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress, the president, their families

drawbacks.text: The rules would not take effect until March 31, 2027, so current officials' trading would continue for years after passage, and officials already in office get a 90-day window to sell with a 120-day compliance runway after that.

The ban has carve-outs: a spouse may keep stock issued by their own employer or from corporate board service, and small-business stakes are excluded if the ethics office finds no conflict — channels a determined family could still use to hold concentrated positions.

The committee-reported version eliminates qualified blind trusts entirely, so officials with large, complex, or illiquid portfolios must sell outright (extensions capped at 90 days); critics of this approach argue it can deter wealthy private-sector candidates from running and force big asset sales on a fixed clock.

Enforcement depends on the House and Senate ethics offices imposing the monthly penalties and, for trust-communication violations, the Attorney General suing — bodies that under current law have been slow to police members' financial filings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is strong for the public: a modest, well-cushioned cost to a few hundred officials buys a firm ban on the most direct conflict of interest in lawmaking, with tax deferral to soften the divestment and penalties designed to sting. The design flaws are real but secondary — a 2027 start date delays any benefit, the spouse-employment carve-out leaves a channel open, and enforcement leans on ethics offices that would need to actually use the penalty authority. On balance the bill would have done what it promised had it reached a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in December 2024, but Senate leaders never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on April 17, 2023 with 23 Senate cosponsors — 21 Democrats and 2 independents — and it was read twice and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
The bill then sat in committee for over a year; on July 24, 2024 the committee ordered it reported favorably with a substitute amendment, a full rewrite of the original text.

On December 19, 2024, Senator Peters reported the bill with the substitute — which expanded the ban to the president and vice president, added digital assets, phased out blind trusts, and set an effective date of March 31, 2027 — and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 729.

The bill received no Senate floor action in the roughly two weeks between its calendar placement and the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, so it died without any chamber ever voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress, their families, and the president and vice president are better off because the bill died: they keep the ability to own and trade individual stocks, crypto, and derivatives while in office, and financial disclosures remain under the weaker STOCK Act status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members who kept their stock-trading rights

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the ETHICS Act on April 17, 2023 and led it through the two-year Congress.

for.name: 23 Senate cosponsors (21 Democrats, 2 independents)
for.role: Cosponsoring senators, including Sanders, King, Warren, Brown, and Tester
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; none was a Republican.

for.name: Gary Peters
for.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (D-MI)
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill through committee — ordered reported July 24, 2024 and formally reported with a substitute amendment on December 19, 2024, placing it on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote even after it was reported from committee and placed on the calendar in the final weeks of the 118th Congress; the measure died there.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or an independent who caucuses with Democrats — 21 D and 2 I, no Republicans — and although a Democratic-run Senate committee approved the bill, the Democratic Senate leadership never brought it to the floor.

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders (Members of Congress, the president, the vice president, and their families)
industries.note: The bill targets this group directly: it would force them to divest individual stocks, commodities, futures, and (in the reported version) digital assets, with repeating monthly fines for noncompliance. Their interest in keeping those holdings runs against the public's interest in lawmakers who cannot trade on what they know.

Firms would lose members' individual trading accounts and blind-trust management business, but would gain work administering forced divestitures and moving officials' money into diversified funds. The original draft required blind-trust trustees to be financial institutions; the committee substitute dropped that mandate.

The committee substitute added digital assets to the banned 'covered investments', so officials and their families could no longer hold crypto, removing a class of assets lawmakers could currently trade.
